newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists agree to discuss elections.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists agree to discuss elections.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists agreed to discuss early elections on Monday after opposition supporters rallied in the capital and 20 towns across the country.

A party statement said the executive bureau proposed "to accept in principle the idea of holding early parliamentary elections in the context of implementation of a national anti-crisis programme for the economic and financial stabilisation of Bulgaria".

Sofia's rally gathered about 8,000 protesters, far fewer than on Sunday, but tens of thousands turned out in Bulgaria's second city of Plovdiv, home town of president-elect Petar Stoyanov, where the current wave of protests against the ex-communist Socialists began a week ago.
In the port city of Varna, where dockers staged a one-hour warning strike, protesters burned a red communist flag.

Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, said Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov had approached him to offer talks but he insisted that the Socialists must first agree to elections.
"We are not going to discuss anything with them until their Supreme Council firmly declares that they accept the idea of early parliamentary elections," Kostov told the rally.
The Socialist party leadership was meeting to discuss whether to offer elections later this year.

Bulgarian Brady bonds fell on the secondary debt market and traders said they were concerned that the unrest would delay establishment of a tough fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stabilise the economy.

"The Socialists basically failed to proceed with market and structural reforms and especially with privatisation. The country may now default on its Brady debt," said Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics.
"The Socialists would like a second mandate to do the opposite of what they have been doing for two years, but no one believes them now."

About 2,000 students marched through Sofia delivering petitions to Western embassies urging them not to support any new government of the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), which is half way through its parliamentary term.

"We do not want to join the immigrants to your countries, we want a new life here and now," said a declaration delivered to the Italian, Austrian and U.S. embassies, referring to the many young Bulgarians who leave to seek a better life abroad.

The Promyana trade union said miners in the Rhodope mountains were expected to join the dockers on Tuesday. A general strike would be held next week if the Socialists did not yield to the opposition's demands.

"We are preparing a nationwide strike but we would not want to go ahead with it because the economy is in a bad state as it is and such a strike will finish it off," Dimitar Dimanov, deputy president of Promyana, told Reuters.

The main opposition trade union Podkrepa said it would join the warning strike campaign on Wednesday, and other trade union organisations also expressed support. Under Bulgarian law, full strikes require a week's notice.

After demonstrators besieged parliament for 10 hours on Friday and Saturday, Zhelev declined to ask the Socialists to form a new government to replace that of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.

Legally, Videnov's government remains in office until a replacement is formed, but quick formation of a new cabinet is vital to secure a new funding agreement with the IMF and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
Voters delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov as president with 60 percent of the vote. He will be sworn in on January 19.

Annual inflation for 1996 was 310.8 percent, and the Socialists' critics blame the party's powerful business allies for unchecked capital flight which has helped push the lev down to 670 to the dollar from 70 a year ago.
